domain_entities.name: LeaveRequest
attributes: id: string (UUID, generated by the repository)
employeeId: string (the requester; always the actor on create)
leaveTypeCode: LeaveTypeCode (canonical lowercase enum value; carried verbatim on the cancellation notification)
requestedDays: number (canonical inclusive count, never re-derived)
approverId: string | null (the recorded decision-maker; null while DRAFT/SUBMITTED; the notification recipient for an APPROVED cancellation)
cancelledBy: string | null (the actor who cancelled; null until cancelled)
reversesRequestId: string | null (non-null only on a GP-008 reversal row)
domain_entities.purpose: The leave request aggregate root and the subject of every cancellation. This feature adds no field and no state to it; it adds a side effect to two of its existing transitions (SUBMITTED -> CANCELLED in place, and APPROVED -> reversal) and makes its `approverId` load-bearing as the notification recipient for an APPROVED cancellation. `approverId` is the recorded decision-maker and is null until a decision is taken, which is exactly why a SUBMITTED cancellation must resolve its recipient from the employee's manager instead.

domain_entities.name: LeaveRequestReversal
attributes: id: string (a NEW UUID, distinct from the original's)
employeeId: string (copied verbatim from the original)
leaveTypeCode: LeaveTypeCode (copied verbatim; the leave type the cancellation notification must carry)
approverId: string | null (always null — the reversal was never approved)
reversesRequestId: string | null (always the ORIGINAL request id — the only provenance link)
domain_entities.purpose: The GP-008 reversal role of LeaveRequest: a NEW row inserted when an APPROVED request is cancelled, because a completed approval is immutable and must never be written again. It is a domain ROLE, not a separate table or entity type — it is a LeaveRequest row whose `reversesRequestId` is non-null. It matters to this feature because it is the row the cancel operation RETURNS and the row whose `leaveTypeCode` the approver notification must carry, while the notification's `relatedEntityId` and the audit entry's `entityId` stay keyed to the ORIGINAL request id. It is born CANCELLED, terminal and inert: it is never submitted, approved, rejected, cancelled, or reversed again, and it reserves no balance.

domain_entities.name: Notification
attributes: id: string (UUID, generated by the repository)
recipientId: string (the approver — the recorded approverId for an APPROVED cancellation, the requester's direct manager for a SUBMITTED one)
type: string (the notification discriminator; the existing leave notifications use the literal 'leave_request')
message: string (must carry the request id and the leave type so the approver can act without a second lookup)
relatedEntityId: string | null (the ORIGINAL request id — never the reversal row's id)
status: NotificationStatus (defaults to PENDING on create)
domain_entities.purpose: The existing notification entity, reused unchanged in shape. This feature adds a second recipient class to the cancellation path: today a cancellation notifies only the requester; after this feature it also notifies the approver. The entity carries no structured payload field, so the request id and leave type the approver needs must be carried in `message` (and the request id additionally in `relatedEntityId`) — this is the constraint that makes the "carry the request id and the leave type" requirement a domain rule about message content rather than a new field.

domain_entities.name: Employee
attributes: managerId: string | null (the direct-manager link; the sole source of the SUBMITTED-cancellation recipient)
domain_entities.purpose: The approver identity source. This feature reads it in two ways: `managerId` resolves the notification recipient for a SUBMITTED cancellation (the requester's direct manager), and `role`/`id` determine whether the cancelling actor is the recorded approver or an ADMIN acting in their place. No field is added; `managerId` becomes load-bearing on the cancellation path, which is why a null `managerId` is a real domain case rather than a data gap.

domain_entities.name: AuditLog
attributes: entityId: string (the ORIGINAL request id, even on the reversal path)
beforeState: unknown | null (the request as it was before cancellation)
afterState: unknown | null (the cancelled row, or the reversal row)
domain_entities.purpose: The immutable record of the cancellation. This feature explicitly leaves it unchanged: exactly one CANCEL entry per cancellation, same action, same entityType, same entityId (the ORIGINAL request id on both the in-place and the reversal path), same before/after state, written in the same unit of work. It is listed here only to record that the approver notification is an ADDITIONAL side effect and must not be folded into, replace, or duplicate the audit entry.

domain_entities.name: PendingDecision
attributes: status: LeaveStatus (always SUBMITTED while the item is in the queue)
domain_entities.purpose: The approver's own view of the requests awaiting their decision — the read model behind GET /leaves/pending-decisions. It is a projection of LeaveRequest, not a stored entity: it has no id of its own, no table, and no lifecycle of its own beyond membership in the queue. This feature's requirement is a NEGATIVE membership rule: a request leaves the queue the moment it is cancelled, so CANCELLED is never a member state. The projection is derived from the same LeaveRequest rows the rest of the module reads, so the cancellation that removes a request from the queue is the same write that sets status CANCELLED — there is no second source of truth to keep in sync.

business_rules: The approver notification recipient is resolved from the request's status, and from nothing else. For a request cancelled while APPROVED, the recipient is the request's recorded `approverId` — the identity of the person who actually took the decision, read from the request itself. For a request cancelled while SUBMITTED, the recipient is the requester's direct manager, resolved as `employee.managerId` of the request's `employeeId` at the moment of cancellation. The current manager of the requester is NEVER substituted for a recorded `approverId`, and `approverId` is never used for a SUBMITTED request (it is null there by construction). This is the single canonical recipient derivation for every cancellation call site. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever cancellation notification recipient resolution (LeaveRequest -> Employee -> Notification.recipientId) appears, not only here]

Exactly one approver notification is emitted per cancellation, and only for a request cancelled from SUBMITTED or APPROVED. A cancellation from DRAFT notifies no approver at all — matching the existing rule that a DRAFT cancellation touches no balance and no approver ever saw the request. The count is exactly one, never zero and never more than one, for a SUBMITTED or APPROVED cancellation: the notification is not duplicated per approver candidate, not sent to both the recorded approver and the current manager, and not re-sent on a retry of the same cancellation (a repeat cancel of an already-cancelled or already-reversed request fails its state guard and emits nothing). [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever cancellation notification emission (which cancellations notify an approver) appears, not only here]

The approver notification must carry the request id and the leave type, so the approver can act without a second lookup. Because Notification has no structured payload field, the request id and the leave type are carried in `message` (the human-readable text), and the request id is additionally carried in `relatedEntityId` with `relatedEntityType = 'leave_request'`. The leave type carried is the request's `leaveTypeCode` — the canonical lowercase enum value, not a display name and not a re-derived label. On the APPROVED reversal path the leave type is the reversal row's `leaveTypeCode` (copied verbatim from the original) and the request id is the ORIGINAL request id, never the reversal row's id. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever cancellation notification content (Notification.message / relatedEntityId) appears, not only here]

The approver notification is written inside the SAME unit of work as the status change it reports. The cancellation's status write (the in-place `update` to CANCELLED, or the reversal `create`), the balance release, the CANCEL audit entry, the requester notification and the approver notification all execute inside one `IUnitOfWork.withTransaction` callback, with the same `PoolClient` threaded to every participating call. A failure to notify therefore rolls back the cancellation itself, so a cancelled request can never exist with no record of the notification attempt. The notification must not be emitted after the transaction commits, must not be fire-and-forget, and must not be moved to an out-of-band queue in this feature. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever cancellation unit of work (status change + notification atomicity) appears, not only here]

A cancellation writes exactly one CANCEL AuditLog entry and, for a SUBMITTED or APPROVED cancellation, exactly two Notifications: one to the requester (existing behaviour, unchanged) and one to the approver (new). The approver notification is an ADDITIONAL side effect — it does not replace, merge with, or alter the requester notification, and it does not alter the audit entry in any way (same action CANCEL, same entityType 'leave_request', same entityId = the ORIGINAL request id, same beforeState/afterState). A DRAFT cancellation writes one CANCEL audit entry and one requester notification, and no approver notification. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever cancellation side-effect set (audit + notifications) appears, not only here]

A request is a member of the approver's pending-decisions queue if and only if its status is SUBMITTED. CANCELLED is never a member state, so a request leaves the queue the instant it is cancelled — whether it was cancelled in place from SUBMITTED or reversed from APPROVED. Membership is derived from the request's current status on every read; there is no separate queue record to invalidate, no tombstone, and no cached membership. A request that was APPROVED and then reversed was never in the queue at the moment of cancellation (it had already left on approval), so the reversal changes nothing about queue membership — the rule is stated for SUBMITTED because that is the only state a cancellation can remove from the queue. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever PendingDecision queue membership (GET /leaves/pending-decisions) appears, not only here]

The pending-decisions queue is scoped to the requesting approver and reuses the module's existing role-scoped visibility rule rather than defining a second one: an ADMIN sees every SUBMITTED request; a MANAGER sees the SUBMITTED requests of their own direct reports (one level, not transitive) and not their own; an EMPLOYEE sees none. Queue membership (status SUBMITTED) and decide authority are separate concerns — the queue is a view, and the existing decide guards remain the sole authority on whether a decision may be taken. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever PendingDecision queue visibility (which approver sees which request) appears, not only here]

When a SUBMITTED request is cancelled and the requester's `managerId` is null, there is no direct manager to notify. The cancellation itself still succeeds (the status change, balance release and audit entry are unaffected), and the requester notification is still written; only the approver notification is skipped. The approver notification is never addressed to the requester, never addressed to the cancelling actor, and never addressed to an arbitrary ADMIN as a fallback — a notification addressed to the wrong person is worse than no notification. This is a deliberate, narrow exception to the exactly-one rule for SUBMITTED/APPROVED cancellations, and it is the only case in which that rule yields zero.

When the cancelling actor is the same person as the resolved recipient — the recorded approver cancelling an APPROVED request they themselves approved, or a manager cancelling a direct report's SUBMITTED request — the notification is still written. Self-notification is not suppressed: the notification is the durable record that the cancellation happened and that the approver's decision is void, and suppressing it would make the notification set depend on who pressed the button rather than on the state change. The exactly-one rule therefore holds regardless of actor identity.

An ADMIN may cancel an APPROVED request for anyone (exempt from the direct-manager check). The recipient is still the request's recorded `approverId`, not the ADMIN — the ADMIN is the actor, not the approver, and the person whose decision is being voided is the one who must be told. If the ADMIN happens to be the recorded approver, the self-notification rule above applies and the notification is still written.

For a SUBMITTED cancellation the recipient is the requester's manager AS OF the cancellation, resolved live from `employee.managerId` inside the cancellation's unit of work. A manager who has since changed is not notified, and no historical manager snapshot is stored or consulted. This is a deliberate consequence of the recipient rule: a SUBMITTED request has no recorded approver to fall back on, so the live manager link is the only available authority, and the person who would have decided it today is the person who must be told.

For an APPROVED cancellation the recipient is the recorded `approverId` even if that employee has since been TERMINATED or is ON_LEAVE. The notification is addressed to the identity that took the decision, and the recipient's current employment status does not redirect, suppress, or substitute the recipient. The notification is a durable record of the cancellation, not a delivery guarantee to a currently-active inbox.

Self-approval is forbidden by the existing decide guards, so a request can never be APPROVED with `approverId === employeeId`. The APPROVED-cancellation recipient can therefore never be the requester, and the requester notification and the approver notification are always addressed to two different people on that path. On the SUBMITTED path the requester's manager is by construction a different employee from the requester (a self-managing employee is a data anomaly, not a supported case), so the two notifications are likewise distinct. This rule is stated so that no call site needs to de-duplicate recipients.

The SUBMITTED-cancellation recipient is the requester's `managerId` regardless of that employee's `role`. The manager link, not the role enum, is the authority for who would have decided the request — the existing decide guard already requires a MANAGER to be the requester's direct manager, so a `managerId` pointing at a non-MANAGER is a data anomaly that the notification path does not attempt to correct or second-guess. No role check is applied when resolving the recipient.

The SUBMITTED-cancellation recipient is the requester's `managerId` regardless of that employee's `role`. The manager link, not the role enum, is the authority for who would have decided the request — the existing decide guard already requires a MANAGER to be the requester's direct manager, so a `managerId` pointing at a non-MANAGER is a data anomaly that the notification path does not attempt to correct or second-guess. No role check is applied when resolving the recipient.

A cancellation notification is created in status PENDING and is never advanced to SENT by the cancellation operation. There is no delivery step in this feature: the notification's existence inside the committed unit of work IS the record of the notification attempt, and PENDING is the honest state for a notification that has been recorded but not delivered. The cancellation must not fail, retry, or block on delivery, and must not mark the notification SENT or READ. Advancing PENDING -> SENT is a separate, out-of-band concern owned by the notification module and is out of scope here. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever Notification.status lifecycle on the cancellation path appears, not only here]

The SUBMITTED-cancellation recipient is the requester's `managerId` regardless of that employee's `role`. The manager link, not the role enum, is the authority for who would have decided the request — the existing decide guard already requires a MANAGER to be the requester's direct manager, so a `managerId` pointing at a non-MANAGER is a data anomaly that the notification path does not attempt to correct or second-guess. No role check is applied when resolving the recipient.

The approver notification reuses the existing notification `type` value used by every other leave notification (the literal 'leave_request') and introduces no new type value, no new enum member, and no new discriminator. The approver notification is distinguished from the requester notification by its recipient and its message text, not by its type. This keeps every existing consumer of the notification feed working unchanged and avoids a second, parallel notification taxonomy for the same entity. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever Notification.type discriminator on the cancellation path appears, not only here]

The SUBMITTED-cancellation recipient is the requester's `managerId` regardless of that employee's `role`. The manager link, not the role enum, is the authority for who would have decided the request — the existing decide guard already requires a MANAGER to be the requester's direct manager, so a `managerId` pointing at a non-MANAGER is a data anomaly that the notification path does not attempt to correct or second-guess. No role check is applied when resolving the recipient.

This feature changes no authorization and no timing rule. Who may cancel is unchanged: the owner may cancel their own DRAFT or SUBMITTED request; only the requester's direct manager or an ADMIN may cancel an APPROVED request; cancellation is blocked once `startDate <= today` (UTC day comparison) with ConflictError. The notification is a consequence of a cancellation that has already been authorized — it must never be used to widen who may cancel, to grant an approver a cancellation right, or to make an unauthorized cancellation succeed. A rejected cancellation emits no notification of any kind. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever cancellation authorization and timing guards appears, not only here]

The SUBMITTED-cancellation recipient is the requester's `managerId` regardless of that employee's `role`. The manager link, not the role enum, is the authority for who would have decided the request — the existing decide guard already requires a MANAGER to be the requester's direct manager, so a `managerId` pointing at a non-MANAGER is a data anomaly that the notification path does not attempt to correct or second-guess. No role check is applied when resolving the recipient.
domain_notes:
## Domain slice — Notify the approver when a leave request is cancelled

### Entities (7)
`LeaveRequest` (15 fields, unchanged shape), `LeaveRequestReversal` (a domain ROLE of LeaveRequest — a row with non-null `reversesRequestId` — not a new table or type), `Notification` (unchanged shape, reused), `Employee` (unchanged; `managerId` becomes load-bearing), `AuditLog` (unchanged by explicit requirement), `PendingDecision` (new read-model projection behind GET /leaves/pending-decisions; no id, no table).

### Lifecycle states — every state named for architectureMdUpdate
- **LeaveRequest**: `DRAFT`, `SUBMITTED`, `APPROVED`, `REJECTED`, `CANCELLED` — unchanged set. New binding semantics: `APPROVED` is terminal/immutable (GP-008); `DRAFT` and `SUBMITTED` are mutable and cancelled in place.
- **LeaveRequestReversal**: `CANCELLED` — single state, born CANCELLED, never transitions. Terminal and inert: never submitted/approved/rejected/cancelled/reversed again, reserves no balance.
- **Notification**: `PENDING`, `SENT`, `READ`, `ARCHIVED` — unchanged. A cancellation notification is created `PENDING` and is NOT advanced by this feature (no delivery step; PENDING is the honest state for a recorded-but-undelivered notification).
- **AuditLog**: `RECORDED` — unchanged, terminal, immutable.
- **Employee**: `ACTIVE`, `TERMINATED`, `ON_LEAVE` — unchanged; a TERMINATED recorded approver is still the notification recipient.
- **PendingDecision** (NEW): `AWAITING_DECISION` (status SUBMITTED), `RESOLVED` (left the queue — by decision or by cancellation). CANCELLED is never a member state.

### Named transitions
- `cancelInPlace`: `DRAFT -> CANCELLED` (no balance touch, no approver notification) and `SUBMITTED -> CANCELLED` (releases `pendingDays`; emits the approver notification).
- `reverseApproved`: `APPROVED -> (original row byte-identical) + new LeaveRequestReversal in CANCELLED`; releases `usedDays`; emits the approver notification keyed to the ORIGINAL id.
- `PendingDecision`: `AWAITING_DECISION -> RESOLVED` on cancellation (this feature's requirement) or on any decision.
- `Notification`: `PENDING -> SENT -> READ -> ARCHIVED` — existing, untouched by this feature.

### Business rules (17 saved)
Broad (binding everywhere the concept is used): recipient derivation by status; exactly-one notification for SUBMITTED/APPROVED cancellations; notification content carries request id + leave type; notification written inside the same unit of work as the status write; side-effect set (1 CANCEL audit + 2 notifications, audit unchanged); queue membership = status SUBMITTED; queue visibility reuses the existing role-scoped rule; notification created PENDING and never advanced; no new `type` discriminator; authorization/timing guards unchanged.
Narrow (single call-site decisions): null `managerId` skips the approver notification; self-notification is not suppressed; an ADMIN cancelling is not the recipient; the live manager is used for SUBMITTED (no historical snapshot); a TERMINATED recorded approver is still notified; requester and approver are always distinct people; the recipient is resolved from `managerId` regardless of the manager's `role`.

### Concerns to surface to the chief architect
1. **`GET /leaves/pending-decisions` does not exist.** A repo-wide search for `pending-decisions`/`pendingDecisions`/`pending_decisions` returns no matches. The existing read surface is `GET /leaves` with a `status` filter plus role-scoped visibility. The feature's requirement ("must stop listing a request once it is cancelled") is therefore a requirement on a NEW read model (`PendingDecision`), not a fix to an existing one. The domain rule is stated as membership = status SUBMITTED, which makes the cancellation requirement fall out for free — but the endpoint itself is new work, and the application architect must decide whether it is a new route or a documented use of `GET /leaves?status=SUBMITTED`.
2. **"the status change" is two different writes.** Because of GP-008, an APPROVED cancellation is not an in-place status change — it inserts a reversal row and leaves the original byte-identical. The atomicity requirement ("sent inside the same unit of work as the status change") must be read as "the status write, whichever form it takes". The existing `LeaveService.cancel` already runs the whole operation in one `withTransaction`, so the requirement is met by extending that callback — but the recipient must be read from the ORIGINAL row, since the reversal row's `approverId` is null by construction. Reading `approverId` off the returned row would silently drop the notification on the APPROVED path.
3. **`Notification` has no structured payload.** The requirement that the notification "carry the request id and the leave type" cannot be met structurally today: the entity has `message` (free text), `title`, `type`, `relatedEntityType`, `relatedEntityId`. The broad rule records the request id in `relatedEntityId` and both values in `message`. If the approver's UI needs the leave type machine-readable, this becomes a change to a shared entity — raised as an open question rather than resolved silently.
4. **A second notification on the same path.** The existing cancel already notifies the requester. This feature adds a second notification to the same unit of work. The audit entry is explicitly unchanged (one CANCEL entry, `entityId` = the ORIGINAL request id on both paths) — the approver notification is additive and must not be folded into it.
5. **`docs/DOMAIN.md` is stale** (it still records `LeaveRequest.leaveTypeId`, `approvedBy`/`approvedAt`, `EmploymentStatus.INACTIVE`, and an `audit` section with `oldValues`/`newValues`/`performedBy`/`performedAt`). The built entity shapes above are authoritative; the drift predates this feature and is recorded so the next reader is not misled.

### Open questions (5)
Null `approverId` on a legacy APPROVED row; self-notification suppression; structured vs free-text leave type on the notification; whether the pending-decisions queue is status-only or decide-scoped; and whether the reversal path notifies the original's approver keyed to the original id (the current broad rule) or is treated as a distinct event.

open_questions.question: An APPROVED request whose `approverId` is null has no recorded approver to notify. The architecture records that `approverId` was only populated on approve/reject in a follow-up fix phase, so APPROVED rows written before that fix can legitimately carry a null `approverId`. What should the cancellation do?
open_questions.impact: The APPROVED-cancellation recipient rule ("the recorded approverId") has no value to resolve, so the exactly-one-notification rule cannot be satisfied. This is not the same case as a null `managerId` on the SUBMITTED path, because the request DID have a decision-maker — the identity was simply never persisted. Choosing wrong either silently drops the notification the feature exists to send, or addresses it to someone who never decided the request.
candidate_options: Skip the approver notification (same treatment as a null managerId) and let the cancellation succeed
Fall back to the requester's current direct manager, on the grounds that they are the person who would decide it today
Fail the cancellation with ConflictError, forcing the null approverId to be repaired first
Backfill approverId for legacy APPROVED rows in a migration before this feature ships, making the case unreachable

open_questions.question: Should the approver notification be suppressed when the cancelling actor is the resolved recipient (the recorded approver cancelling their own approval, or a manager cancelling a direct report's SUBMITTED request)?
open_questions.impact: Determines whether the notification set depends on actor identity or purely on the state change. Suppressing it makes the "exactly one notification per SUBMITTED/APPROVED cancellation" rule conditional and harder to assert; not suppressing it means a user can receive a notification about their own action. The narrow rule recorded above currently says self-notification is NOT suppressed, but this is a product judgement rather than a derivable fact.
candidate_options: Always notify, even when actor === recipient (recorded as the current narrow rule)
Suppress the approver notification when actor === recipient, keeping the requester notification
Always notify but mark the notification as self-authored so the UI can de-emphasise it

open_questions.question: The approver notification must "carry the request id and the leave type", but Notification has no structured payload field — only `message` (free text), `title`, `type`, `relatedEntityType` and `relatedEntityId`. Is carrying the leave type inside the human-readable `message` text acceptable, or does the approver view need it machine-readable?
open_questions.impact: If the approver's UI must render the leave type as a structured field (a badge, a filter, a link), a free-text message cannot serve it and the Notification entity needs a new field — which is a domain change to a shared entity, not a local one. If free text is acceptable, the requirement is satisfied with no entity change and the rule stays a content rule. This also decides whether the leave type is duplicated into `relatedEntityType` (currently reserved for the entity discriminator 'leave_request') or left only in the message.
candidate_options: Carry both in the free-text `message`; no entity change (the current broad rule)
Add a structured payload field to Notification (e.g. `payload: unknown | null` or `metadata`) and carry requestId + leaveTypeCode there
Reuse `relatedEntityType` to carry the leave type and keep only the request id in `relatedEntityId`
Add a dedicated `leaveTypeCode` field to Notification

open_questions.question: Does GET /leaves/pending-decisions need to exclude requests the caller may not decide (e.g. a MANAGER's own SUBMITTED request, or a SUBMITTED request whose requester is not their direct report), or is it purely a status-filtered list?
open_questions.impact: The feature's stated requirement is only that a cancelled request stops being listed. But the queue is named "pending-decisions", which implies the items are decidable by the caller. If the queue is status-only, a MANAGER can see their own SUBMITTED request in a list they cannot act on; if it is decide-scoped, the queue must re-express the decide guards (no self-approval, direct-manager-only) and stay consistent with them. This decides whether the queue is a thin status filter or a second expression of the authorization rule.
candidate_options: Status-only: every SUBMITTED request visible under the existing role-scoped visibility rule, regardless of decidability
Decide-scoped: exclude the caller's own requests and, for a MANAGER, requests whose requester is not their direct report
Status-only now, with the decide-scoping deferred to a follow-up feature

open_questions.question: Should the approver notification be emitted when an APPROVED request is cancelled via the GP-008 reversal path, given that the reversal row is a NEW row and the original APPROVED row is left byte-identical?
open_questions.impact: The feature description says "on cancellation of a SUBMITTED or APPROVED request, send one notification to the approver", which covers the APPROVED path — but the APPROVED path is now a reversal, not an in-place cancellation, and the reversal row carries a null `approverId` by construction. The recipient must therefore be read from the ORIGINAL row, and the notification's `relatedEntityId` must be the ORIGINAL id, not the reversal's. Getting this wrong either drops the notification entirely (reading `approverId` off the reversal row, which is always null) or points the approver at a row they never decided.
candidate_options: Notify the original's recorded approver, keyed to the ORIGINAL request id (the current broad rule)
Notify the original's recorded approver but key the notification to the reversal row id
Do not notify on the reversal path — treat the reversal as a distinct event with its own notification semantics
